# dev-prune (devp)

> A Rust CLI that reclaims disk space from idle Git repositories by deleting dependency
> and build directories — `node_modules`, `.venv`, `target`, `vendor` and whatever else
> its twenty-four supported package managers own — but only after the project's own
> package manager confirms a lockfile can rebuild them. Apache-2.0,
> no analytics and no diagnostics; the only network request is an opt-out release
> check against GitHub. Windows, macOS, Linux.

Version 1.16.0. Written by VKrishna04.
Repository: https://github.com/Life-Experimentalist/dev-prune
Homepage: https://devprune.vkrishna04.me
JSON Schema for `.devprune.json`: https://devprune.vkrishna04.me/schemas/v1/devprune.schema.json
Full CLI reference: https://devprune.vkrishna04.me/reference/

## What it is

`dev-prune` is the binary; `devp` is the same executable under a second name, and both
work in every shell. It registers Git repositories, judges each one idle from `git log`
commit timestamps *and* source file modification times, asks each package manager to
verify its lockfile, and only then deletes. `devp restore` puts everything back.

It covers the whole disk side of dependencies, not deletion alone: `devp run` prunes,
`devp restore` and `devp undo` reverse it, `devp caches` sizes and clears the caches
package managers keep outside projects, `devp containers` reports Docker's, `devp status`
and `devp stats` show where the space went and is going (filterable by drive), and
`devp doctor` and `devp trust` audit the installation itself. One tool for every
dependency directory on the machine rather than one per ecosystem.

The core bet: a `node_modules` in a project you have not touched for weeks is a cache,
not data — the lockfile is the data. dev-prune deletes only what a lockfile can
provably regenerate, and treats "provably" literally: the package manager itself is run
in a read-only verification mode before anything is removed, and a verification that
fails, times out, or would need to rewrite the lockfile is a refusal.

## Why it exists / when to use it

- A development machine accumulates tens or hundreds of cloned repositories; each
  JavaScript project can hold 0.2–2 GB of `node_modules`, each Rust project multiple GB
  of `target`. Most are idle. dev-prune reclaims that space without deleting anything
  unrecoverable and without the user remembering which projects are safe.
- It runs unattended (OS scheduler + Git hooks that auto-register new clones), so the
  reclaiming keeps happening after the first run.
- Use `devp run --dry-run` to see what a pass would free; `devp status` for the
  interactive dashboard; `devp stats` for what has already been reclaimed over time;
  `devp history` for which pass reclaimed it and what started that pass.

When NOT to use it: it never deletes build *outputs* (`dist/`, `.next/`, compiled
artifacts) on a rule of its own — those are not provably rebuildable from a lockfile, so
there is no detection rule for them and there will not be one. Two things sit outside
that: the opt-in cargo/gradle/maven/swift adapters, whose build trees are provably
regenerated by recompiling the sources sitting next to them and which stay off until you
switch them on; and directories a repository *declares* through `prunable.directories`
(see below), where the required `rebuild` command supplies the proof a lockfile
cannot. It is not a generic disk cleaner: directories outside registered Git
repositories are never touched. Machine-wide package caches are *reported* by
`devp caches` (with the vendor's own clear command) and never deleted by anything that
runs on its own, because a shared cache cannot be proven recoverable by any one lockfile
and it is what makes restore fast. Container engines are reported the same way by
`devp caches docker`, and nothing that runs on its own will ever touch one.
`devp caches clear <manager>` empties a cache when you type it, and
`devp caches clear <engine>` runs Docker's or Podman's own narrow prune commands when you
name the engine — both after showing what goes and asking, and neither ever touching a
volume, which is the one thing here that nothing can hand back.

## Install

- Linux, macOS, and Windows under Git Bash/MSYS2/Cygwin:
  `curl -fsSL https://devprune.vkrishna04.me/install.sh | sh`
- Windows PowerShell: `iwr -useb https://devprune.vkrishna04.me/install.ps1 | iex`
- Windows Command Prompt: `powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Command "iwr -useb https://devprune.vkrishna04.me/install.ps1 | iex"`
  (same install; `devp` resolves in the next Command Prompt, not the current one)
- npm: `npm install -g dev-prune`, or `npx dev-prune status` to run it once without
  installing. Works on Windows from 1.8.0 onwards; `dev-prune@1.7.0` and earlier
  installed on Windows and then reported no binary to run, and a published manifest
  cannot be edited, so those machines need `npm install -g dev-prune@latest`
- bun, pnpm and Yarn: `bun add -g dev-prune`, `pnpm add -g dev-prune`, `yarn global add
  dev-prune` (Yarn 1.x) — the same npm package. dev-prune treats each as a channel of
  its own, not as npm: a copy bun installed is upgraded with `bun add -g
  dev-prune@latest` and removed with `bun remove -g dev-prune`, and running npm against
  it would add a second copy under npm's prefix while bun's stayed stale on PATH
- Python tooling: `uv tool install dev-prune`, `uvx dev-prune status`,
  `pipx install dev-prune`, `pip install dev-prune`
- Cargo, prebuilt: `cargo binstall dev-prune`
- Cargo, from source: `cargo install dev-prune` (Rust 1.88+)
- Homebrew (macOS and Linux): `brew install Life-Experimentalist/tap/dev-prune`
  (the fully-qualified name taps as it installs; no separate `brew tap` step)
- Scoop (Windows): `scoop bucket add life-experimentalist https://github.com/Life-Experimentalist/scoop-bucket`
  then `scoop install dev-prune`
- Homebrew and Scoop also install straight from a URL with nothing tapped or added:
  `brew install https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Life-Experimentalist/dev-prune/main/packaging/homebrew/dev-prune.rb`
  and `scoop install https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Life-Experimentalist/dev-prune/main/packaging/scoop/dev-prune.json`

The Homebrew formula and the Scoop manifest are regenerated by the release itself from
the SHA-256 sidecars it just published, so both spellings always describe the newest
release and each one carries the hash of the archive it installs. The difference is
afterwards: a formula or manifest installed by URL belongs to no tap and no bucket, so
`brew upgrade` and `scoop update` never see a new version. The named tap
(`Life-Experimentalist/homebrew-tap`) and bucket (`Life-Experimentalist/scoop-bucket`)
exist for that, and each pulls its one file from `packaging/` in this repository daily.

`winget install VKrishna04.dev-prune` is submitted and awaiting review
(microsoft/winget-pkgs#422809); every winget-pkgs version is a pull request a person at
Microsoft signs off, so that command starts resolving when it merges and not before.
`brew install dev-prune` with no tap prefix means homebrew-core, which has a notability
bar and is not submitted.

## Editor integration

The companion extension is published as `VKrishna04.dev-prune` on the VS Code Marketplace
(https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=VKrishna04.dev-prune) and on Open VSX
(https://open-vsx.org/extension/VKrishna04/dev-prune), which covers VSCodium, Cursor,
Windsurf, Positron and Kiro. It validates `.devprune.json` from a schema bundled inside it
rather than fetched, and puts the workspace's reclaimable size in the status bar. Install
it with `code --install-extension VKrishna04.dev-prune`, or let `devp setup` offer it.

JetBrains IDEs need no extension: the config schema is registered with SchemaStore, so
IntelliJ, PyCharm, WebStorm, GoLand, RubyMine, Rider, Visual Studio, Neovim and Zed
validate `.devprune.json` out of the box. `devp skill --agent <editor>` writes the rules
file a coding agent in that editor actually reads.

The PyPI packages contain the prebuilt binary rather than downloading one at install
time, so they install correctly behind a registry mirror and with no network access.
`cargo install` is the only channel that compiles on your machine — crates.io
distributes source, so there is no binary there for cargo to fetch. `cargo binstall`
reads the `[package.metadata.binstall]` table in `Cargo.toml` and downloads the GitHub
release archive instead, needing no toolchain.

Both installers take `--version`/`-Version`, `--bin-dir`/`-BinDir`, `--no-path`/`-NoPath`,
`--no-auto-setup`/`-NoAutoSetup`, `--force`/`-Force` and `--help`/`-Help`. Piping into a
shell has nowhere to put an argument, so passing one means `… | sh -s -- --no-auto-setup`
or `& ([scriptblock]::Create((iwr -useb …))) -NoAutoSetup`; the equivalent environment
variables (`DEV_PRUNE_VERSION`, `DEV_PRUNE_BIN_DIR`, `DEV_PRUNE_NO_PATH=1`,
`DEV_PRUNE_NO_AUTO_SETUP=1`, `DEV_PRUNE_FORCE=1`) work with the plain one-liner, and a
flag wins over its variable.

Each installer asks exactly one question, and only when another package manager's copy is
on PATH: whether to collapse the two by running `devp install --channel installer --yes`
from that older binary, which is the copy that knows which manager owns it. Anything but
`y` prints the command instead, and the question is skipped — the command still printed
— with `DEV_PRUNE_NO_MIGRATE_PROMPT=1` set, with `CI` set, or with no terminal attached
at all, which covers container builds and CI. Neither script ever deletes another
manager's file. Each finishes by writing `install.json` beside the binary: schema,
version, channel, which script wrote it, when, the executable path, and whether `devp` and
the PATH entry came from it. `devp doctor` reports it as an **Install receipt** line and
plain `devp install` prints the same summary. It is a record, never a setting: nothing
reads it to decide anything, `Channel::detect()` still classifies a copy by where its file
is, and a copy from any other channel simply has none.

Re-running either one-liner is safe and does only what needs doing. An install already at
the version being installed, with `devp` beside it and on PATH, is left untouched and
exits 0 without downloading; an older one is updated in place; a newer one is not
downgraded unless the version is named with `--version`/`-Version`; and a same-version
install missing `devp` or its PATH entry is reinstalled, which repairs both.
`--force`/`-Force`/`DEV_PRUNE_FORCE=1` downloads and writes both files regardless.

The installers verify the published SHA-256 checksum and refuse to install without one.
Seven prebuilt binaries cover everything: Windows, macOS and Linux on x64 and arm64,
plus a 32-bit windows-x86 build for machines with no 64-bit mode (there is no 32-bit
Linux, macOS or ARM build). The Linux builds are statically linked against musl, so there
is no per-distribution asset and no glibc floor — one file per architecture runs on
Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, RHEL, Arch, NixOS and Alpine.

## Commands

- `devp init [PATHS]` — crawl for Git repositories and register them, then run the setup
  pass. `devp init --auto` works the paths out instead of being told them and `PATHS` is
  ignored: the parent directory of every repository already registered (the source that
  reaches repositories outside the home directory, on a second drive), the workspace you
  are standing in, and the conventional code directory names under your home directory
  (`Code`, `Projects`, `Developer`, `Development`, `dev`, `src`, `repos`, `git`, `work`,
  `workspace`, `Documents/GitHub`, `source/repos`, `go/src`). A root that lies inside
  another root is dropped so a tree is walked once, and the home directory itself is
  never a root, because scanning it would walk every cache on the machine. The same 8
  levels, and it works with `--dry-run`. Aliases: `scan`, `onboard`. A bulk scan — `devp
  init` with or without `--auto` — will not register a repository holding an
  `ignore.devprune.json`, so a repository can decline before it is ever registered rather
  than only at prune time; `devp link` still registers one, because naming a single
  repository is not a bulk scan
- `devp link [PATH]` / `devp unlink [PATH]` — register or unregister one repository;
  `devp unlink --missing` drops every entry whose directory no longer exists
- `devp undo` — revert the most recent `init` or `link`
- `devp run [PATH]` — prune every registered repository, or one target. Both forms
  list what would go, with sizes and the total, and ask before deleting; `-y` answers,
  `--dry-run` stops at the report, and without a terminal the run exits with an error
  naming `--yes` rather than waiting on a prompt
- `devp status [--top N] [--drift] [--json]` — interactive dashboard; a plain table when
  there is no TTY. In the dashboard `s` cycles the sort (relevance, size, longest idle,
  name), `f` cycles the filter (all, candidates, has bloat, problems) and `/` searches
  paths and adapter names; all three change only what is shown, never the totals. `--top N` lists only the N repositories with the most reclaimable
  space; the totals above the table still cover every registered repository. Above the
  table, once this machine has timed a restore with `devp restore --last-run`, `status`
  also estimates how long putting everything back would take, split by adapter; the
  timings are local and never uploaded, and the line is absent rather than guessed until
  there is a measurement. `--drift`
  replaces the dashboard with the lockfile-drift report: every environment holding
  packages its lockfile never recorded (`npm install --no-save`, a bare `pip install`
  into a pinned venv, an ad-hoc `uv pip install`), with the one command that records
  them — a pure read, and the same comparison a prune refuses on
- `devp stats [--json]` — what has already been reclaimed: lifetime total from pruning,
  a separate one from `devp caches clear <manager>`, and a third from `devp caches clear
  <engine>` (never added together: one costs a reinstall in one repository, the next a
  download in every project, the last a pull of the whole layer stack), prune passes,
  the most recent pass and how to undo it, the repositories that gave back the most,
  which package managers those reclaims came from, and how the passes were started
  (`manual`, `scheduled` or `dashboard`, each printed even at zero — a `scheduled` line
  reading zero passes is how you learn the daemon is not running).
  Per-repository figures and the pass history are recorded from 1.1.0 onward; the two
  breakdowns from 1.17.0, since they are summed from the prune log. The manager
  breakdown covers pruning only — a cache clear is not a pass — so it does not add up
  to the lifetime total, and each breakdown reports how many passes it could not count
- `devp history [--pass N] [--limit N] [--all] [--json] [--export [PATH]]` — which pass
  deleted what, and what asked it to. `stats` says ten passes freed 27 GiB; this says
  that pass #2 ran at 09:14 as `devp run --daemon`, took 4.02 GiB out of two
  repositories, and names all three directories. Bare, it is one line per pass — when,
  what started it (`manual` for a typed `devp run`, `scheduled` for the background pass,
  `dashboard` for the `[p]` key in `devp status`, and there is no fourth), how much, and
  how many directories in how many repositories. `--pass N` opens one in full: the exact
  command line, the version that ran it, and every directory removed with its package
  manager and size, grouped by repository. Read-only. The log is `prune-log.jsonl`
  beside the registry, holding the 100 most recent passes; nothing depends on it, and
  `devp restore --last-run` reads the registry rather than this. Per-directory detail is
  recorded from 1.17.0 onward — older passes still appear with their totals, marked
  `(totals only)`, and carry `detail: false` in `--json`. On a terminal the directory
  list of one pass is capped at 200 entries and says how many were left out; redirected
  or piped, nothing is elided. `--export` writes the JSON document to a file — with a
  path, exactly that path; bare, to the user's documents folder
- `devp completions <bash|zsh|fish|powershell|elvish>` — print a shell completion script
  to stdout, generated from the same argument definition the binary parses with
- `devp caches [--volume <VOLUME>] [--json]` — find and size every package-manager cache and store on the
  machine (npm, pnpm, yarn, bun, uv, pip, conda, cargo, go, maven, gradle, nuget,
  vcpkg, conan, composer, cocoapods, hex, bundler, dart, swift, terraform, poetry, pdm,
  playwright, puppeteer, huggingface, cypress, electron, deno), largest first, with two
  commands per row:
  `devp caches clear <manager>` and, below it, the manager's own command that dev-prune
  runs for it. Both, because they are not synonyms — what dev-prune clears is added to the
  lifetime cache total in `devp stats`, and the same command typed into a terminal is
  invisible to it. Maven prints only its own command; dev-prune will not run that one. The report deletes nothing, and no
  scheduler, Git hook or `devp run` ever will: a cache is shared by every project, so no
  one lockfile can prove it recoverable, and it is what makes `devp restore` fast. This is also where the
  .NET and C/C++ ecosystems are covered — their in-repository `bin/`+`obj/` and CMake
  `build/` directories are compiler outputs no lockfile can prove rebuildable, so
  dev-prune never deletes them, while their dependencies live in these machine-wide
  stores. Cargo `target/`, Maven `target/` and Gradle `build/`+`.gradle/` are the one
  exception, via the opt-in adapters below. `devp config set cache_max_gb default=10`
  writes down how big is too big, in gibibytes (GiB, the unit the report
  prints), for every manager at once, and a manager past its cap
  is marked in the report — measured against the manager's whole footprint, so cargo's
  registry cache and its unpacked sources are weighed together. Setting a cap still
  deletes nothing; it marks, and `devp caches clear --over-cap all` empties exactly what
  is marked, when you type it. Empty by default: no cache is too big until you say what
  too big is. Each manager also carries how many registered repositories use it and what
  its cache works out to per repository — two repositories sharing a 12 GiB cache is 6 GiB
  each and worth a look, forty sharing the same 12 GiB is the cache doing its job. A
  manager no registered repository uses at all is the one case a count is enough to act on,
  and `devp caches clear --unused all` empties exactly those. The count ignores whether an
  adapter is enabled, because the question is which managers the projects *use*, not which
  ones a prune pass would touch, and it is shown only for the nineteen managers that are
  also adapter names — the other ten (`pip`, `conda`, `nuget`, `conan`, `hex`,
  `playwright`, `puppeteer`, `huggingface`, `cypress`, `electron`) have no adapter of the
  same name, so dev-prune says nothing about them rather than guessing that `venv` feeds
  `pip` or that every `node_modules` on the disk feeds the Playwright browser cache.
  The browser, model and Electron caches are there because each routinely reaches
  gigabytes and nothing ever removes an old entry: Playwright and Puppeteer keep a whole
  browser build per version, Cypress an unpacked Electron app per version, and
  `huggingface` is the one row where re-downloading is measured in tens of gigabytes and
  can fail outright — a gated or now-private repository will not hand the weights back. With no registered
  repository on disk nothing is counted and `--unused` refuses to run, because every cache
  would otherwise look unused. pnpm gets a row per filesystem rather than a single row:
  it hardlinks its store into every `node_modules` it fills and a hardlink cannot cross
  a filesystem, so projects kept off the system disk have a store of their own at the
  root of that filesystem — `V:\.pnpm-store` on a second Windows drive,
  `/mnt/data/.pnpm-store` on Linux, `/Volumes/Work/.pnpm-store` on macOS — and `pnpm
  store path` only ever answers for the filesystem it is run on. dev-prune looks at the
  root of every filesystem holding a registered repository, plus the current one, and
  each such row names its store in the command it prints: `pnpm store prune --store-dir
  <path>`
  Which brings up the drive question generally: the report ends with a `By drive` line
  splitting the total per volume, largest first, and every row in `--json` carries a
  `volume` key naming the drive or filesystem it sits on. `devp caches --volume V:`
  narrows the whole report to one of them — `--drive` is the same flag, and it also takes
  a mount point (`/mnt/data`, `/Volumes/Work`) or any path on the drive you mean,
  including `.`. On a machine whose projects live on a second disk the machine-wide total
  is not the figure that decides anything; the gigabytes on the drive that is full are.
  The narrowing happens last, after every verdict, so a `cache_max_gb` cap still measures
  a manager's whole footprint wherever it is and a cache no registered repository uses
  does not become unused merely because the repositories that use it are on another
  drive. Container engines are left out of a filtered report entirely, and the `json`
  document omits `containers` rather than emitting an empty list: an engine reports its
  disk from inside a VM image with no path on this filesystem, so it belongs to no drive.
  `--volume` paired with `clear`, `docker` or `containers` is a usage error rather than a
  flag that looks accepted and does nothing — the clear commands empty a manager wherever
  it is, which for every manager but pnpm is one place.
- `devp caches docker` / `devp caches podman` / `devp caches containers [ENGINE]`
  `[--json]` — what a container engine is holding: images, containers, local volumes and
  build cache, each with a count, a size, and how much of that size the engine says it
  could give back. Then the prune commands that would give it back, narrowest first, with
  what each takes with it. **This report deletes nothing**, and no scheduler or Git hook
  reaches container disk at all — that part is permanent. `devp caches clear <engine>`
  runs the narrow ones for you when you name the engine; see below. The figures
  come from the engine's own `system df` rather than a directory walk, because on Docker
  Desktop and Podman the store lives inside a VM disk image the host filesystem cannot
  see — a size taken off the disk would be wrong by orders of magnitude, in the
  reassuring direction — and because asking is the only way to learn what is
  *reclaimable*, which is the figure that decides anything: 40 GB of images with 38 GB
  dangling is a different situation from 40 GB with 2 GB dangling. An engine that is
  installed with its daemon stopped is reported as exactly that, quoting the engine's own
  first line, and contributes no figures — a blank, not a zero, and `--json` omits the
  size keys rather than sending `0`. An engine that is not installed is absent rather than
  listed as missing. Local Kubernetes clusters (kind, k3d, minikube) are listed by name
  and deliberately not sized: they run their nodes as containers belonging to an engine
  already in the table, so a figure beside the cluster name would be the same gigabytes
  twice; the names are read out of your kubeconfig, which contacts nothing. `devp caches`
  itself prints one summary line per engine under its table, outside its own total —
  container disk is not a package manager cache and adding the two figures together is
  always wrong. Exit 0 whether an engine answered, was stopped, or was not installed;
  2 for an engine name it does not know
- `devp caches clear <docker|podman|nerdctl|finch|container> [--dry-run] [--yes] [--json]`
  — run the narrow prune commands the report above prints, after printing them and asking:
  `builder prune -a -f`, `image prune -a -f` and `container prune -f` for docker and
  podman, and `system prune -a -f` for nerdctl and finch, whose narrow subcommands are
  spelled differently across versions. Apple's `container` gets `image prune -a` and
  `prune`: it has no `system prune`, and its prune subcommands neither ask a question nor
  define a `-f`, so those two run the moment they are typed — the confirmation is
  dev-prune's own, and the report says so before the list. **No volume, ever**: there is no argument anywhere in that
  table containing the word, and a unit test fails the build if one appears. That is not
  the lockfile rule — an image can be pulled again and a build cache rebuilt, so those are
  a question of consent, and the prompt is the consent — it is that a named volume holds
  the only copy of what is inside it. The headline estimate has the engine's unused-volume
  figure subtracted out and names it separately as left alone, pointing at
  `<engine> volume prune` as yours to type. Freed space is `system df` before minus after,
  never the sum of what the commands claimed: layers are shared, so those add up to more
  than the disk ever held. It is counted on its own line in `devp stats`. Not reachable
  from `clear all`, from any scheduler, or from a Git hook — naming the engine is the
  consent. An engine that is not installed, or whose daemon is stopped, is exit 2 quoting
  the engine's own words rather than a guess. `--over-cap` and `--unused` with an engine
  name are exit 2: an image belongs to no repository and `cache_max_gb` does not cover one
- `devp caches clear <manager|all> [--over-cap] [--unused] [--dry-run] [--yes] [--json]` — empty one manager's
  cache, or every one of them, after listing and sizing what goes and asking. A
  convenience, never automation: only this command clears a cache, and only when you
  type it. It runs the manager's own subcommand wherever one exists (`npm cache clean
  --force`, `pnpm store prune`, `go clean -modcache`) because the manager knows what is
  still referenced; only cargo, gradle, vcpkg and hex, which ship nothing
  equivalent, are cleared by removing the directory this command already resolved and
  sized. conda's `conda clean --packages --tarballs --yes` keeps whatever its
  environments reference through a hardlink, and conda documents that it does not
  check for packages an environment linked by symlink instead — an environment broken
  that way reinstalls from the channel it came from, so the row says so rather than
  refusing. Maven is the exception in the other direction: `~/.m2/repository` is an install
  target as well as a download cache — `mvn install:install-file` puts artifacts there
  that exist in no remote at all — so dev-prune sizes it, prints
  `rm -rf ~/.m2/repository`, and refuses to run it. `clear maven` is a usage error that
  says why; `clear all` skips it and says so, and the `--json` documents carry it under
  `kept`. A
  manager that is not installed is reported as failed, never deleted around. The freed
  size is measured afterwards rather than assumed. `--json` requires `--yes`; exit 1 if
  any cache could not be cleared, 2 for an unknown manager name or for `maven`
- `devp trust [--json | --fix-ownership [--yes]]` — what dev-prune is allowed to do on this machine, on one
  screen. Three sections: the guarantees the code enforces on every machine (the seven
  safety invariants, no telemetry, build outputs never deleted, container disk never
  deleted — none with a setting or
  a flag behind it), and this machine read live (scheduler, Git hooks, registered
  repository count, idle window, managed binary path, and the three settings that widen
  anything: `require_confirmation=false`, `allow_manifest_rewrite`, and
  any opt-in adapter: `enable_cargo`, `enable_gradle`, `enable_maven`,
  `enable_swift`, `enable_dart`, `enable_mix_build`, `enable_vcpkg`,
  `enable_cmake_build`), and every executable dev-prune owns on this machine — the one
  running marked and listed first, each with its SHA-256 and a VirusTotal lookup URL for
  that digest, because an antivirus judges the bytes on your disk rather than the asset
  on a release page. Those links are lookups by hash, computed locally and printed, never
  fetched and never an upload; a digest the service has not seen returns "not found",
  which means unscanned, not clean. On Windows `dev-prune.exe` and `devp.exe` share a
  digest on purpose (one file, two names, one reputation record) and `devpw.exe`, the
  console-free build the scheduler runs, is a separate build target that legitimately
  differs. A release-installed copy matches the published `.sha256` and the per-file
  `.zip.contents.sha256` manifest; a `cargo install` build matches nothing published.
  No letter grade — the widened settings are named, because
  "trust level: MEDIUM" tells nobody which switch to look at. Read-only, always exit 0.
  The binaries section lists *every* copy of `dev-prune`, `devp` and `devpw` on the
  machine — everything on `PATH` plus each channel's install directory even when it is
  no longer on `PATH` — with the version it was built as, the manager that installed it
  (`channel`), its SHA-256 and a VirusTotal lookup URL for that digest, running copy
  first. The version is read out of the file's own bytes, never by running it, so it is
  absent for anything built before 1.17.0; the highest copy is marked `latest release`
  when a release check has confirmed that is the newest release and `newest here` when
  it is only the highest version on this machine. Several copies is normal
  and not a fault: a `cargo install` and an installer run each leave one and they update
  separately, which is why their digests can differ. Shims (`.cmd`, `.ps1`) are excluded
  because hashing a text wrapper answers nothing. Nothing found is executed, only hashed
  `--fix-ownership` is the one exception: it adds every registered repository Git
  currently refuses to read — the "detected dubious ownership" refusal, routine after a
  Windows reinstall or a restored backup — to the global `safe.directory` list, after
  printing the full list and asking; `--yes` answers that for a script. It matters
  because dev-prune dates a repository by its last commit, so one Git will not read has
  no known age and is never pruned
- `devp restore [PATH]` — reinstall dependencies for every project in a tree;
  `devp restore --last-run` restores exactly what the most recent prune pass deleted.
  A pruned virtual environment records the Python that built it and is rebuilt on that
  same interpreter; if it is no longer installed the restore asks once, defaults to no,
  and names the `uv python install` command that fixes it
- `devp doctor [PATH] [--fix]` — diagnose the installation, or one repository with a path
  (`devp doctor .` names the reason a prune pass would skip it); read-only, runs no
  package manager, repairs nothing. `devp doctor --fix` then repairs what the checks
  found, for installed-but-broken integrations only — a stale `devp` twin, hooks or a
  scheduler entry pointing at a binary that no longer exists, a drifted hook chain, a
  missing `SKILL.md` export, registry entries whose repository is gone. Each repair is
  the corresponding setup pass re-run, so it can never do more than `devp setup` would,
  and it never performs a first-time install
- `devp config …` — global settings, per-repo config, scheduler, hooks, file-manager icons;
  `devp config wizard` walks every setting and runs itself on the first install;
  `devp config recommended [--with-cautious]` applies the recommended tier in one
  non-interactive command
- `devp setup [--status]` — install any missing integration; `--status` only reports
- `devp skill [--agent <editor>]` — export `SKILL.md` and install it into a detected
  agent skills directory (`~/.claude/skills/dev-prune/`); prints onboarding prompts for
  agents without one. `--agent` writes per-repository rules for one editor instead.
  Ten write a file of their own: cursor (`.cursor/rules/dev-prune.mdc`), windsurf
  (`.windsurf/rules/`), antigravity (`.agent/rules/`), cline (`.clinerules/`), roo
  (`.roo/rules/`), kilocode (`.kilocode/rules/`), continue (`.continue/rules/`),
  amazon-q (`.amazonq/rules/`), kiro (`.kiro/steering/`) and trae (`.trae/rules/`).
  Six share a file with other tools and get a marked block inside it: agents-md
  (`AGENTS.md`, read by Codex, Jules, Amp and OpenCode), copilot
  (`.github/copilot-instructions.md`), gemini (`GEMINI.md`), junie
  (`.junie/guidelines.md`), zed (`.rules`) and aider (`CONVENTIONS.md`). Aider is
  the one target that does not read its file by finding it — `read:
  CONVENTIONS.md` in `.aider.conf.yml`, or `aider --read CONVENTIONS.md`, is what
  loads it, and the command prints that after writing
- `devp update [--offline | --install | --channels]` — print the installed version, check GitHub for a newer release, and show the upgrade command. `--install` downloads the release binary for this platform from GitHub Releases, refuses it unless its SHA-256 matches the published sidecar, and writes it to every copy this installation runs: the managed binary under the config directory, its `devp` alias, the windowless `devpw` scheduler twin, and the running binary. The package manager that delivered the first copy is deliberately not run — its version record goes stale and the single command that resyncs it is printed — and its own upgrade command is the fallback when no binary is published for this platform or the download fails. `auto_update`, on by default, does the verified-download half by itself at the end of a prune pass — never the package-manager half, which can prompt, and nothing at all on WinGet, Scoop and Homebrew, where the manager owns the upgrade; `devp config set auto_update false` stops it. An upgrade never interrupts the scheduler. `version_lock`, off by default, outranks all of it: with `devp config set version_lock true` this copy stays on the version it is — `auto_update` does not run however it is set, `--install` and `devp install --channel` refuse, and a re-run of the install one-liner leaves the binary alone. No flag bypasses it; `devp config set version_lock false` is the way back, and every path that stands down prints the pin rather than going quiet. `DEV_PRUNE_OFFLINE=1` in the environment keeps the process off the network entirely, regardless of any setting. `--channels` prints the upgrade command for every channel dev-prune ships through instead of only the one that owns this copy — no network, nothing read, nothing written, and not combinable with `--offline` or `--install`
- `devp install [--channel <NAME>] [--dry-run]` — move this installation from one package manager to another. `devp update` upgrades the copy that is running, through whichever channel installed it; this changes *which* channel owns it. It installs through the manager named first and removes the old copy through the manager that put it there second, so a failed install leaves the working copy untouched. Removing the old copy through its own manager rather than deleting the file is the point: a manager whose record still says dev-prune is present will put the old binary back. Names: `installer`, `cargo`, `npm`, `bun`, `pnpm`, `yarn`, `uv`, `pipx`, `winget`, `scoop`, `homebrew` — bun, pnpm and yarn install the same npm package but are each their own channel, because each keeps its own record of what it installed, so a copy bun put there is upgraded and removed with bun. With no `--channel` it reports which manager owns the running copy; `--dry-run` prints the numbered plan and runs none of it; `--yes` skips the confirmation. Nothing is migrated because nothing needs to be — settings, the registry and the undo history live in the config directory, which no package manager owns. Running the `install.sh`/`install.ps1` one-liner over an existing install from any other channel is a different thing and is safe: it never fails because of the older copy and never deletes it, it puts its own directory first on PATH (prepended to the rc file on macOS and Linux, prepended to the User PATH on Windows) so the copy it just wrote is the one that answers, and it names the other one and asks whether to collapse the two, running `devp install --channel installer --yes` from that older copy if you answer `y` and printing the command otherwise
- `devp man [command] [--dir <dir>] [--roff]` — the manual, generated from the same clap
  definitions `--help` uses. At a terminal, `devp man` prints the contents page: every
  command grouped by what it is for with one line each, the flags that go before the
  command, and the exit codes. `devp man <command>` prints one command's page — the same
  text `devp <command> --help` prints. Roff appears only where something can format it:
  a redirect or a pipe gets roff (`devp man | man -l -`, `devp man > devp.1`), and
  `--roff` forces it at a terminal too. `--dir` writes the full set, one page per
  subcommand plus `devp.1` and `dev-prune.1`
- `devp uninstall [--deep]` — remove the program: scheduler, hooks, agent skill, PATH
  entry and the binaries themselves, then a sweep over PATH and the well-known install
  dirs (`~/.cargo/bin`, `~/.local/bin`, npm global, venv Scripts) removes every other
  copy after one confirmation (`-y` covers it; non-interactive without `-y` skips the
  sweep with a note). Manager-owned copies get the exact uninstall line printed so the
  manager's records clear too; `--deep` also clears config. On Windows a running
  binary cannot delete itself, so the running copy is renamed aside and the remains
  queued for the next restart — no helper process is left behind, and exit `1` means
  something is still installed under its original name
- `devp -V` — version plus an environment audit

Global flags: `--dry-run`, `--ignore-idle` (`--force` is the deprecated alias),
`-y`/`--yes`, `--json` on the reporting commands (`run`, `status`, `stats`, `trust`, `caches`).
Piped `--json` output is one document on stdout and nothing else; only when stdout is
an actual terminal is the document also copied to the human's clipboard (stderr note).
`devp run --except <name>` prunes everything *but* the named repositories, which is the
usual way to keep one project warm. `devp run --only <adapter>` / `--skip <adapter>`
narrow a pass to named ecosystems. `devp run --explain` lists every repository and
directory with the reason it would or would not be pruned — including the states a
normal pass keeps quiet about (still active, opted out, under the size floor);
read-only, and it conflicts with `--json`. A `.` for `[PATH]` means the current directory and
is accepted everywhere a path is.

Exit codes are a contract: `0` success, `1` failure (a run in which any repository
failed exits `1` even if others succeeded), `2` unusable arguments. `devp doctor` exits
`0` for warnings and `1` only for genuine breakage.

## The seven safety invariants

Enforced in code, with no bypass flag — full detail with the exact commands in
https://github.com/Life-Experimentalist/dev-prune/blob/main/docs/SAFETY_INVARIANTS.md:

1. **`.git` boundary** — nothing outside a directory containing a `.git` folder is ever
   processed. Linked worktrees and submodule checkouts (a `.git` *file*) are refused,
   conservatively.
2. **Lockfile pre-verification** — before deletion, the ecosystem's manager runs a
   read-only check (`npm ci --dry-run --ignore-scripts`,
   `pnpm install --lockfile-only --frozen-lockfile`,
   `bun install --frozen-lockfile --dry-run --ignore-scripts`, `uv lock --locked`,
   `cargo metadata --locked`, `go mod download`, …) under a timeout. If the manager is
   missing but a lockfile exists, the lockfile itself is the proof. A drifted lockfile
   is a refusal, not something to quietly fix: rewriting forms
   (`cargo generate-lockfile`, `go mod tidy`, …) run only when no lockfile exists at
   all, or after the explicit opt-in `devp config set allow_manifest_rewrite true`.
   The venv adapter runs nothing: it requires `requirements.txt` to list at least one
   package and refuses when the environment holds packages the file never recorded.
3. **Idleness** — `max(last commit, newest source mtime)` must be older than
   `idle_days` (default 15). `--ignore-idle` lifts this check and nothing else.
4. **Atomic state writes** — the registry is written to a temp file and renamed, never
   edited in place; a crash mid-write leaves the previous state intact.
5. **Opt-outs** — `ignore.devprune.json` in a repository root is honoured by file
   presence alone (0 ms, nothing parsed), at registration as well as at prune time: a
   bulk scan (`devp init`, with or without `--auto`, and the scheduled pass's own
   discovery) will not register a repository holding it, while `devp link <path>` still
   does, because naming one repository is not a bulk scan. `"ignore": true` in
   `.devprune.json` does the same after a parse. A `.devprune.json` that does not parse skips the repository and
   reports the error — defaults are never guessed for a file that said something.
6. **Symlink refusal** — a bloat directory that is a symlink or Windows junction points
   at storage the repository does not own (typically a monorepo's real `node_modules`)
   and is refused, never followed. The directory walk never follows links either.
7. **Nested-repository boundary** — discovery walks at most `scan_depth` levels
   (default 6, max 32), never descends into `node_modules`/`target`/`vendor`/venvs or
   hidden directories, and never crosses into a nested `.git` repository — a submodule
   or vendored checkout has its own history and is pruned only in its own right.

Also deliberate: `--dry-run` verifies nothing (it reports sizes and stops before
verification, which is why it is instant), and `.devprune.json` holds inert data only —
no key in it can name a command to run or a path to delete, because the file arrives
with a `git clone` of possibly-untrusted code.

## What it never does

- Never deletes build outputs (`dist/`, `.next/`, `bin/`+`obj/`, compiled artifacts) —
  no lockfile proves them rebuildable.
- Never deletes a machine-wide cache on its own. `devp caches` reports them with each
  vendor's own clear command, and `devp caches clear` empties one only when you type it —
  no scheduler, Git hook or prune pass ever touches one.
- Never deletes container disk on its own. No prune pass, scheduler or Git hook reaches
  an engine, and `devp caches clear all` does not either. `devp caches clear docker` does,
  when you name it and answer the prompt.
- Never deletes a volume, in any command, with any flag. There is no argument in
  dev-prune's container table containing the word "volume", and a unit test fails the
  build if one appears. `docker volume prune` stays a command the report prints and you
  type.
- Never empties Maven's local repository at all. `~/.m2/repository` holds artifacts
  `mvn install:install-file` put there that no remote can hand back, so dev-prune sizes
  it, prints the command, and leaves running it to you.
- Never executes anything named in a repository-tracked file.
- Never rewrites a lockfile during verification, by default in every ecosystem.
- Never edits editor settings, `PATH`, or shell startup files; for editors it prints a
  snippet you paste yourself.
- Never phones home: no analytics, no telemetry; the single network request is the
  opt-out update check against GitHub's public API (no body, no identifier).

## Unicode and non-English paths

Paths are handled as real filesystem paths, never as byte strings, so a repository at
`ワークスペース/项目目录名称测试/프론트엔드` is scanned, verified, pruned and restored
exactly like an ASCII one, on Windows, macOS and Linux alike. Terminal output measures
display *columns* rather than characters, so the tables in `devp status` and
`devp doctor` stay aligned when a directory name is full-width — one CJK character
occupies two columns, and padding by character count is the usual reason a CLI's
columns go crooked. The same applies to accented Latin, Cyrillic, Arabic and emoji
directory names. Program messages themselves are English.

## Supported ecosystems

Twenty-four adapters. npm, pnpm, yarn, bun (`node_modules`); deno (`node_modules`, and
`vendor/` when the config asked for one); uv, poetry, pdm, pipenv
and pip/venv (`.venv`, `__pypackages__`, any directory holding `pyvenv.cfg`); go
(`vendor`); composer (`vendor`); bundler (`vendor/bundle`); cocoapods (`Pods`); mix
(`deps`); terraform (`.terraform/providers`); and, opt-in, cargo (`target/`), gradle
(`build/`, `.gradle/`), maven (`target/`), swift (`.build/`), dart (`.dart_tool/`),
mix_build (`_build/`), vcpkg (`vcpkg_installed/`) and cmake_build (any tree holding a
`CMakeCache.txt`).
The build-tool adapters ship disabled — a build tree is regenerated by recompiling, not
downloading, so they cost more to get back: `devp config set enable_cargo true` /
`enable_gradle true` / `enable_maven true` / `enable_swift true` / `enable_dart true` /
`enable_mix_build true` / `enable_vcpkg true` / `enable_cmake_build true` turns them on, and their candidates wait
for `build_idle_days` (45 by default, applied as the maximum of it and `idle_days`).
`adapter_idle_days` (`cargo=90,npm=30`) raises one named adapter's window further still,
never lowering it. .NET is covered by `devp caches` rather than by an adapter (its
dependencies live in a machine-wide store; its in-repo build directories are outputs,
see above). So is vcpkg in classic mode, where one install tree beside vcpkg itself is
shared by every project on the machine — the adapter claims only manifest mode's
per-project `vcpkg_installed/`. A CMake build tree is claimed only when it proves it is
one: `cmake` writes a `CMakeCache.txt` at the top of every tree it configures and nobody
writes one by hand, and that file records `CMAKE_HOME_DIRECTORY`, the source directory it
was configured from. cmake_build claims a directory only when that recorded source
directory still exists, still holds a `CMakeLists.txt` and sits inside the same
repository, so a `build/` someone made by hand is never touched and the name `build/` is
never what decides. The search stops descending at the first cache it finds, so the
sub-builds `FetchContent` and CPM leave under `build/_deps/` go with the tree that
configured them, and it reaches three levels down because Visual Studio's CMake
integration configures into `out/build/<preset>/`.

Bundler and pipenv claim only the install that lives inside the repository: the
`vendor/bundle` that follows `bundle config set path vendor/bundle`, and the `.venv`
that appears under `PIPENV_VENV_IN_PROJECT`. Both tools default to a shared store under
the user's home directory, which dev-prune never touches — neither as a prune nor
through `devp caches`, because that directory is where other projects' dependencies are
installed rather than a cache. Composer declines `vendor/` entirely when a
`vendor/bundle` is inside it, because no `composer install` puts those gems back. The always-on mix adapter
takes `deps/` and never `_build/`, and the opt-in mix_build adapter takes `_build/` and
never `deps/`; swift takes `.build/` and never `.swiftpm/`; dart
takes `.dart_tool/` and never `build/`. Terraform takes `.terraform/providers` and
nothing else under `.terraform/` — `environment` records the selected workspace and
losing it silently returns you to `default`, `terraform.tfstate` is the backend's
initialisation record, and `modules/` comes from sources the lock file says nothing
about.

cocoapods, mix, mix_build, dart, terraform, gradle, maven, swift, vcpkg and cmake_build
verify offline: their ecosystems have no read-only in-sync command, and the write-side ones fix
drift by re-downloading, so what is checked is that the lockfile is structurally
complete and no older than the manifest it came from, or that the build manifest the
tree is derived from is present and parses. vcpkg additionally requires a non-empty
`dependencies` list, because every vcpkg *port* also carries a `vcpkg.json` and a port
manifest rebuilds nothing. cmake_build requires the `CMakeLists.txt` its build tree names
to be readable and to actually declare a project.

Any of the twenty-four can be switched off with `disabled_adapters`.

A repository may hold any number of these, at the root or up to `scan_depth` levels
below it. Where several managers claim the same `node_modules`, the owner is chosen
from the `packageManager` field, else the bookkeeping files inside the installed tree,
else the most recently written lockfile. uv wins over plain venv when `uv.lock` or
`[tool.uv]` is present.

Sizing is honest about hardlinks (1.1.0): under pnpm and bun, files hardlinked into the
manager's global store are excluded from the reported reclaimable size — deleting
`node_modules` removes the link but the store keeps the bytes. The excluded amount is
reported separately (`shared_bytes` in `--json`). Copied installs (exFAT, cross-volume
stores, macOS clonefile) count in full. The prune itself always removes the whole
directory; hardlink awareness changes accounting, never what is deleted.

## Configuration

Global settings live in `%APPDATA%\dev-prune` (Windows),
`~/Library/Application Support/dev-prune` (macOS), `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/dev-prune` (Linux).
Thirty-one keys, all readable with `devp config get <key>` and writable with
`devp config set <key> <value>`. They fall into seven groups, and `devp config wizard`
walks them in this order:

**The language this is all in** — which catalogue dev-prune's own headings and
summary lines come from: `language` (en).

**What gets pruned** — the size and age of what a pass considers at all:
`idle_days` (15), `min_size_mb` (0), `scan_depth` (6), `disabled_adapters` (none),
`adapter_idle_days` (none).

**Before anything is deleted** — the checks between a candidate and a deletion:
`require_confirmation` (true), `allow_manifest_rewrite` (false),
`command_timeout_secs` (600).

**Build trees** — off by default, because everything here comes back by
recompiling rather than downloading: `enable_cargo` (false), `enable_gradle` (false),
`enable_maven` (false), `enable_swift` (false), `enable_dart` (false),
`enable_mix_build` (false), `enable_vcpkg` (false), `enable_cmake_build` (false),
`build_idle_days` (45).

**Shared download caches**: `cache_max_gb` (none).

**Running without being asked** — what may be installed on the machine, and how
often it may act alone: `auto_setup` (true), `auto_config` (false),
`auto_daemon` (true), `auto_discover` (true), `check_interval_days` (2),
`auto_hooks` (true), `auto_hooks_chain` (false).

**Keeping dev-prune current**: `update_check` (true),
`update_check_interval_days` (7), `update_check_timeout_secs` (5),
`auto_update` (true), `version_lock` (false).

`command_timeout_secs` bounds one package-manager command dev-prune itself runs — the
lockfile check before a delete, and the reinstall `devp restore` performs. Nothing is
compiled under it: the opt-in build adapters run no command at all during a prune,
because a build tree needs no lockfile proof. The single exception is a restore whose
install builds a native module.

`auto_discover` lets the scheduled background pass — `devp run --daemon`,
the one the OS scheduler starts — look for unregistered repositories by itself, using the
same roots as `devp init --auto`, and register what it finds. A manual `devp run` never
does, and `devp config set auto_discover false` turns it off. It widens what is
*registered*, never what is deleted: a newly registered repository is pruned only once it
is idle past `idle_days`, only where a lockfile proves every candidate directory can be
rebuilt, and only after the seven safety invariants pass, so the worst a wrong guess
costs is an extra row in `devp status`. A repository holding an `ignore.devprune.json` is
not registered at all.

`auto_hooks_chain` is off because `core.hooksPath` is one slot, global to the machine,
and often already held by husky, pre-commit or lefthook. On, dev-prune installs in
front of the existing path and forwards every hook on to it; off, it declines the slot
and `devp doctor` prints the command to enable chaining if that is wanted.

`disabled_adapters` is a comma-separated list of adapter names to leave alone
entirely: a disabled adapter is not detected, not counted by `stats`, not probed for
by `doctor` and never pruned, as if that ecosystem were not installed on the machine.
`devp config set disabled_adapters -` clears it. It is a deny-list rather than
twenty switches because the answer for almost everyone is "none", and it is
separate from `enable_cargo` / `enable_gradle` / `enable_maven` / `enable_swift` /
`enable_dart` / `enable_mix_build` (Elixir: Mix is Elixir's build tool, and
`_build/` holds the compiled project, separate from the downloaded `deps/` the
always-on `mix` adapter claims) / `enable_vcpkg` / `enable_cmake_build`,
which are off because of what their directories cost to rebuild rather than because
anyone dislikes them.

`cache_max_gb` is a per-manager ceiling in gibibytes (GiB, the unit the report
prints), written `default=10,npm=4`. It is
keyed by the names `devp caches clear` takes — `npm`, `pnpm`, `uv`, `pip`, `cargo`,
`go`, `nuget` and the rest — not by adapter name, because the two lists overlap
without either containing the other. `default` is the extra key: it covers every
manager not named separately, so one entry caps all twenty-nine caches, and a manager
named outright is held to its own figure rather than to both. A manager over its cap is marked in `devp caches`
and cleared only by `devp caches clear --over-cap`; the cap itself never deletes
anything. `devp config set cache_max_gb -` clears the map.

`language` picks which of twelve catalogues dev-prune prints its own headings and
summary lines from: `en`, `zh` (Simplified Chinese), `hi` (Hindi), `te` (Telugu),
`ta` (Tamil), `kn` (Kannada), `ml` (Malayalam), `bn` (Bengali), `mr` (Marathi),
`gu` (Gujarati), `pa` (Punjabi), `sa` (Sanskrit). Nothing a script reads moves with it — `--json`, exit codes, flag
names, config keys and adapter names are English in every catalogue — and a key a
catalogue has not translated falls back to English rather than printing blank.
`DEV_PRUNE_LANG=te devp run` overrides the setting for one command; the operating
system's locale is deliberately never consulted, so the choice is made once by a
person and stays made. English is the only catalogue a native speaker has reviewed;
`devp config set language <code>` says so when the one you picked has not been.

`devp config wizard` opens all thirty-one in a full-screen configurator, one
category per screen — the
`devp trust` declaration first, then every setting, then a summary of exactly what
will be written. Enter is the "keep going" key: it takes the safe recommendation on
the row it is on and moves to the next, so holding it walks the whole list, and on
the Finish line it opens that summary — one more Enter saves. The walk starts at the
top and visits every row. The walk never takes
the cautious tier (`allow_manifest_rewrite`); that stays a deliberate Space. `a`
takes every remaining safe recommendation at once and jumps to the summary — the same
set the walk would have taken, cautious tier still excluded; Shift+Enter is the same
thing on terminals that report the modifier. It runs
itself once on a first install and again after an upgrade adds a setting the machine
has never been shown, marking that one `NEW`; settings already confirmed are never
re-asked. `--no-tui` or `DEV_PRUNE_NO_TUI=1` asks one question per line instead,
where saving takes two empty lines. Agents should use `devp config set`, which needs
no terminal at all.

`devp config recommended` is the non-interactive shortcut: it applies everything the
first run recommends without a caveat — `enable_cargo`, `enable_gradle`,
`enable_maven`, `enable_swift`, `enable_dart`, `enable_mix_build`, `enable_vcpkg`,
`enable_cmake_build`, and `cache_max_gb=default=10`. That last one is the only
suggestion that is not a yes-or-no, so any ceiling already set counts as taken: a
machine with `npm=4` is left alone rather than overwritten. `allow_manifest_rewrite` is a second tier of one, held back
unless `--with-cautious` is passed, because it lets `cargo` and `go` edit files Git
tracks. `devp config show` lists whatever is still outstanding. Neither marks the
settings reviewed, so the walkthrough a machine is owed still opens.

Per repository: `ignore.devprune.json` in the root is an instant opt-out;
`.devprune.json` supports `project_name`, `ignore`, `disable_daemon`, `disable_hooks`,
and the three overrides `override_idle_days`, `min_size_mb`, `scan_depth`. Files
written by `devp config project` carry a `$schema` link, and the schema is published at
https://devprune.vkrishna04.me/schemas/v1/devprune.schema.json for editor IntelliSense.
The other global settings have no per-repository form deliberately — a repository config
can arrive in a clone somebody else wrote, so a repository must not be able to grant
itself `allow_manifest_rewrite`. Every one of these files holds inert data only.

`devp config project <PATH> --team` creates `project.devprune.json`: the same keys and
the same schema, meant to be committed, and so deliberately not written into
`.git/info/exclude` the way `.devprune.json` is. Where both exist, every key the project
file names wins and the personal file answers every key it does not — the inverse of the
usual local-overrides-shared convention, because these are decisions a project makes and
"this repository is not worth pruning" should survive a colleague's stale local file. A
key the project file does not literally contain decides nothing, which is why `--team`
creates it holding only its `$schema` line. `devp config project <PATH>` prints an
Effective values table naming which file each value in force came from. dev-prune's own
writes — `--update`, the workspace toggles, `i` in the dashboard — only ever touch
`.devprune.json`, never the committed file.

Either file may also carry `"prunable": {"directories": [...]}`, naming directories no
adapter can recognise — each an object with `path` (repository-relative), a required
`rebuild` command, and an optional `why`. Use `"rebuild": "echo not needed"` when nothing
has to rebuild it. These are pruned by the ordinary pass under the adapter name
`declared`, so they obey `--dry-run`, `--min-size`, `--only` and the schedule. Unlike
every other key the two files' lists add up rather than one winning.
`"prunable": {"exclude": [...]}` names declared paths to leave alone on this machine,
whoever declared them — the way to keep a directory the committed file calls rebuildable
without editing a file the whole team shares. Spelled the same way as a `path` (trailing
slash, leading `./` and backslashes all match), honoured from whichever file names it
because a veto only ever deletes less, and the entry it names is skipped entirely rather
than reported. Naming one path in both lists of the same file is a typo, not a decision:
the exclusion wins and the declaration never runs, and `devp doctor` says so. All three
config files are read from the repository root only, because the paths inside them are
relative to it — a copy in a subdirectory parses and does nothing, which `devp doctor`
warns about without moving it. Because the
committed file arrives in a clone, each declaration is checked before anything is
deleted: relative path with no `..`, resolving inside the repository even through a
symlinked parent, holding no Git-tracked file, and a `rebuild` whose first word is a
program on this machine. A declaration that fails is reported as `skipped_declaration`
and nothing is deleted. dev-prune prints the rebuild command and never runs it.

## Machine-readable output (for tools and AI agents)

Add `--json` to `run`, `status`, `stats`, `trust` or `caches` for a versioned JSON document
(`schema` 1, additive changes only within a major version). Highlights:

- `devp status --json` — per-repository totals, per-directory sizes, and status
  (candidate / active / ignored / no_bloat / path_missing / config_error). `totals.restore_estimate`
  and each repository's `restore_estimate_secs` are null until a restore has been timed
  on that machine.
- `devp run --json` — one result per repository × directory with the action taken or
  the refusal reason; refusals include the exact fix command where one exists
  (e.g. the lockfile-repair command for that ecosystem). `size_freed` counts only bytes
  deletion actually returns; `shared_bytes` is what hardlinked stores keep.
- Exit codes carry meaning (see above), so scripting on them is supported.

For AI coding assistants there is a dedicated skill file:
`devp skill` exports it locally, and the canonical copy is
https://github.com/Life-Experimentalist/dev-prune/blob/main/.agents/skills/dev-prune/SKILL.md
— a task-to-command table (including "is this safe?" answers), the JSON field
reference, and the failure playbook. Agents should prefer `--json` over parsing the
human report, use `--dry-run` before a destructive suggestion, and never suggest
`--ignore-idle` without asking the user first.

## Background automation

The `devp` second binary, the managed binary directory on `PATH` (a user `PATH` entry
on Windows, `~/.local/bin` symlinks elsewhere — this is what keeps a pip-in-venv
install working after the venv is gone), the exported `SKILL.md`, the skill installed
into any detected agent skills directory, global Git auto-registration hooks,
the OS scheduler and the file-manager icons install themselves at install time, and
again on `devp init` or after an upgrade if any of them is missing. `devp setup` runs
the same pass by hand and `devp setup --status` only reports. Hooks are skipped when
`git` is not on `PATH`. When the global `core.hooksPath` already belongs to husky,
pre-commit or lefthook, the pass skips the hooks and says so; `devp hook install --chain`
takes the slot and writes shims that `exec` the displaced directory's same-named hook,
so both run. An unchained install shims every hook name too, forwarding to the
repository's own `.git/hooks`, so setting `core.hooksPath` does not disable a repo-local
pre-commit gate. Chaining is opt-in — `auto_hooks_chain` defaults to false. The setup
pass registers no repository itself; the scheduled prune pass is where that can happen,
and only while `auto_discover` is on (the default), where it looks for unregistered
repositories using the same roots as `devp init --auto` and registers what it finds — a
manual `devp run` never does, a repository holding an `ignore.devprune.json` is never
registered, and being registered still only means being considered, not pruned.
`devp config set auto_discover false` turns it off. Turn any of it
off with `auto_setup`/`auto_hooks`/`auto_hooks_chain`/`auto_daemon`/`auto_discover`, or
`DEV_PRUNE_NO_AUTO_SETUP=1` in the environment, which switches off all five at once. Everything the setup pass writes lives
under your own config and data directories and is removed by `devp uninstall`.

## Guides

Long-form answers to the questions that lead people here, at
https://devprune.vkrishna04.me/blog/ :

- /safe-to-delete-node-modules/ — is it safe to delete `node_modules`, and how to check
- /delete-node-modules-all-projects/ — clearing `node_modules` across a whole machine
- /reclaim-disk-space-developer-machine/ — where a developer machine's disk actually goes
- /clear-package-manager-cache/ — the right clear command for thirteen managers
- /delete-venv-safely/ — deleting `.venv` for uv, Poetry, PDM, Pipenv and plain venv
- /cargo-target-directory-size/ — why Rust's `target/` grows, and what to delete
- /vs/ — an honest comparison with kondo, npkill, cargo-sweep, rimraf and a cron job
